{"id": "89:17/q02", "question": "On what basis are people honored or humiliated, and why is provision varied?", "turns_on": "The notes contrast decree without stated cause, hidden benefit, and testing, while also identifying obedience and treatment of the vulnerable as measures of standing.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q02/p1", "position": "Honor is through obedience or piety and disgrace through disobedience or sin.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers Qatāda because the ensuing neglect of the orphan and poor shows the ground of humiliation. The divine saying cited by al-Qurṭubī contrasts obedience and sin. Al-Nasafī phrases honor as being enabled to obey and humiliation as abandonment. Biqāʿī says treatment of orphans shows the real measure; love or aversion to worldly life signals disposition to sin or obedience."}, {"id": "89:17/q02/p2", "position": "Provision follows divine decree, power, will, and judgment beyond human causal explanation.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī presents this as the Sunni account, and Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Bursevī say neither wealth nor poverty is assigned to prove personal merit or contempt. Al-Qurṭubī also attributes both conditions to decree."}, {"id": "89:17/q02/p3", "position": "Provision follows hidden beneficial purposes known only to God.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī presents this as the Muʿtazilite account. Ibn ʿĀshūr says divine dealings have purposes beyond ignorant conjecture and calls for reasoning guided by revelation."}, {"id": "89:17/q02/p4", "position": "Both abundance and restriction are tests of gratitude, patience, and conduct toward others.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes gratitude and obedience for the rich from gratitude and patience for the poor. Al-Nasafī cites 21:35 on testing with good and evil, and 28:78 against entitlement. Iṣlāḥī says favors test service to others while hardship tests contentment; the peaceful soul succeeds. Qur'an Yolu adds sharing and organized solidarity."}, {"id": "89:17/q02/p5", "position": "Restriction can itself honor by turning a person toward God, while abundance can entrap or ruin.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says constriction can expiate sin or restrain desire and prosperity can be gradual enticement. Al-Bursevī reports that deprivation may keep blessings from distracting from their Giver; his report of seventy impoverished Companions of the Bench illustrates poverty without humiliation. A spiritual master sees the claim 'my Lord humiliated me' as a veil over merciful movement from nature to spirit, self to heart, and separation to union."}, {"id": "89:17/q02/p6", "position": "Honoring, urging, eating, and loving are human acts for which people are praised or blamed.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī infers human agency from the praise and blame attached to the four actions."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q03", "question": "How should a person respond to prosperity and hardship?", "turns_on": "The sources stress either praise and patience in both conditions or the social duties that wealth makes possible.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q03/p1", "position": "Give thanks and obey in prosperity; remain grateful and patient in hardship.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and those reporting him stress praise in both states. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn Kathīr add obedience and patience. Al-Bursevī cites a hadith that faith is half patience and half gratitude."}, {"id": "89:17/q03/p2", "position": "Use prosperity to fulfill others' rights, particularly those of orphans and the poor; endure deprivation without despair.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī describes proud Makkan and Ṭāʾif leaders whose wealth should have led to gratitude and service. Qur'an Yolu joins sharing and organized solidarity with patience and reverence for God's command. Al-Māwardī is not in these notes."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q04", "question": "How does kallā function as a stop or opening?", "turns_on": "Whether kallā is heard as closing the prior claim or emphatically opening the next sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q04/p1", "position": "It can close the preceding false claim, and stopping here is preferred.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports Makkī's first category: denial of what precedes permits a stop at kallā, preferred at eleven locations including al-Fajr; it cites 19:15, 23:100, 34:27, 70:39, 74:32, 83:14, and 104:4."}, {"id": "89:17/q04/p2", "position": "Restarting at kallā can make it an emphatic opening.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports this as the alternative to stopping on the denial."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q05", "question": "What does bal do in the move to the orphan rebuke?", "turns_on": "Whether the transition emphasizes escalation to worse acts, correction of the supposed cause of disgrace, or sentence structure.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q05/p1", "position": "It moves from a false statement to worse conduct: wealthy people neglect the orphan's due.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ālūsī stress the escalation; abundance creates a duty to give, and their failure is worse than their mistaken words. Al-Ālūsī says direct address intensifies censure. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the shift by contrast to their boast of divine favor and generosity while they hoard surplus."}, {"id": "89:17/q05/p2", "position": "It turns from the claim of humiliation by restricted provision to the actual fault, neglect of orphans.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī points to 89:18 as confirming this cause; al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī put the fault on the people's own behavior."}, {"id": "89:17/q05/p3", "position": "It introduces a new sentence, either opening discourse or parenthetically separating the two kallā statements.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr describes both discourse opening and parenthesis as syntactic possibilities."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q06", "question": "How does the plural address relate to the earlier singular human?", "turns_on": "The choice between a direct turn to humanity, an implied 'say,' and continued third-person reference to collective al-insān.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q06/p1", "position": "The discourse shifts to direct plural address of humanity as a collective, making the rebuke more forceful.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī observes the address; al-Fārisī explains agreement by grammatical form versus collective meaning and cites 7:4. Al-Samīn, Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr describe the genus-to-plural shift; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it confrontation of the offenders."}, {"id": "89:17/q06/p2", "position": "The second person may be an implied command to the Prophet: 'Say this to them.'", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī and al-Rāzī give this rationale; al-Ālūsī reports that supplying qul removes a grammatical shift while retaining censure."}, {"id": "89:17/q06/p3", "position": "The third person continues the generic collective 'human' and informs the Prophet and believers about their conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, and al-Samīn connect the plural to al-insān. Al-Fārisī and al-Wāḥidī cite 7:4 for shifting by sense; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 90:6–7."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q07", "question": "How are 'you do not honor' and the following verbs read?", "turns_on": "Whether the verbs confront listeners with tāʾ or report their conduct with yāʾ; the notes give reader lists and prophetic transmission for the alternatives.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q07/p1", "position": "They are read with second-person tāʾ, confronting the audience.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names Abū Jaʿfar and most Kufans; other lists name Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, or the non-Basrans. The variant covers the four verbs of honoring, urging, eating, and loving, though al-Fārisī lists three. Al-Durr reports ʿĀṣim with lengthened unhamzated taḥāḍḍūn and geminated lamman. Al-Nashr excepts al-Zubayrī from Rawḥ from the Basran third-person group."}, {"id": "89:17/q07/p2", "position": "They are read with third-person yāʾ, reporting 'they do not honor' and continuing the earlier collective referent.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb or the Basrans are named most often; Bayḍāwī adds Sahl. Al-Ālūsī lists al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Abū Rajaʾ, Qatāda, and al-Jaḥdarī. Reports ascribe yāʾ to prophetic recitation through ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf (authenticated by al-Ḥākim), Abū Hurayra, and Ibn ʿUmar. The listed verbs usually run through love in 89:20. Qiraat-ER notes that prefix and person change while form and object remain."}, {"id": "89:17/q07/p3", "position": "The established regional forms are all valid in meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī permits recitation with any of three established regional readings; Study Quran says either person reading is accepted."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q08", "question": "What does 'the orphan' denote here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q08/p1", "position": "A child who lost his father before adulthood; the definite singular denotes orphans collectively.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds that for an animal, orphan denotes loss of its mother. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the generic definite and compares his discussion at 4:2. Al-Bursevī likewise specifies a human orphan who lost a father before maturity."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q09", "question": "Which individual is reported as the orphan behind this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q09/p1", "position": "Qudāma ibn Maẓʿūn was an orphan under Umayya ibn Khalaf, who withheld his right.", "reasons": "Muqātil is named as the reporter in al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, and al-Qurṭubī. Name spellings vary slightly; some reports say this was the occasion of revelation."}]}

Al-Jishumī includes care of person and property because of the orph

{"id": "89:17/q11", "question": "What duty and wider moral lesson does the orphan rebuke teach?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis is the immediate duty to an orphan or the social and spiritual failure the neglect reveals.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q11/p1", "position": "People must honor vulnerable orphans and safeguard their persons and property.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī infers the positive duty from the prohibition of dishonor. Al-Biqāʿī says their inability to repay favor exposes selfish motive. Al-ʿĀshūr adds material support, kind treatment, and protection of feelings. Al-Malı emphasizes using present opportunity for good before the afterlife."}, {"id": "89:17/q11/p2", "position": "Failure toward orphans and the poor exposes greed, neglect of the Hereafter, and failed stewardship of wealth.", "reasons": "Muqātil connects neglect to disbelief in the Hereafter. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ links oppression and corruption to greedy individualism dulling conscience and insight. Qur'an Yolu criticizes polytheist arrogance, selfishness, and attachment to wealth while presenting compassion as a religious duty."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q12", "question": "What prophetic reports commend honoring or caring for an orphan?", "turns_on": "The reports differ between the worth of a household's treatment and the caregiver's promised closeness to the Prophet.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q12/p1", "position": "The most beloved or best home honors an orphan; the worst home mistreats one.", "reasons": "The 'most beloved home' wording is reported from ʿUmar and elsewhere without a named transmitter; al-Suyūṭī marks it sound in Ibn ʿAṭiyya's note, while Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī give no grading. Abū Hurayra's report in Ibn Kathīr contrasts best and worst Muslim homes."}, {"id": "89:17/q12/p2", "position": "The Prophet and an orphan's caregiver will be close together in Paradise like the index and middle fingers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports the gesture; Ibn Kathīr gives transmissions from Abū Hurayra and Sahl ibn Saʿd, naming both fingers."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q13", "question": "How do the neighboring poor and inheritance clauses explain this rebuke?", "turns_on": "Whether the next verses chiefly clarify omitted duties, identify inheritance abuses, or tie the social rebuke back to the false divine-honor claim.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q13/p1", "position": "Failure to urge feeding the poor accompanies failure to honor the orphan, and can imply failing to feed the poor oneself.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites 89:18 as evidence that disgrace comes from conduct. Al-Bayḍāwī says the wealthy do not even urge family to feed. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees reciprocal ellipsis: failing to honor also means failing to urge guardians, while failing to urge feeding implies failing to feed from one's wealth. Rāzī distinguishes Muqātil's 'not feeding' from his own 'not urging others.'"}, {"id": "89:17/q13/p2", "position": "The inheritance and wealth verses expose the material form of mistreating orphans and greed.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and al-Rāzī use 89:19 for withholding inheritance; al-Rāzī uses 89:20 for merging orphan wealth with one's own. Ibn ʿĀshūr links the transition to their boast of generosity."}]}
{"id": "89:17/q14", "question": "What expressions and readings in the neighboring clauses bear on this passage?", "turns_on": "The notes treat separate forms in adjacent verses as contextual evidence for the orphan rebuke.", "positions": [{"id": "89:17/q14/p1", "position": "The phrase about 'food of the poor' means feeding the poor through ellipsis or use of food for feeding.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī supplies an omitted verbal noun as one analysis and treats 'food' itself as standing for the act of feeding as another."}, {"id": "89:17/q14/p2", "position": "The reciprocal verb for urging can reflect loss of one initial tāʾ; its reading varies in vocalization and length.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī derives the reciprocal from tatafāʿalūn and notes a reading with ḍamma on tāʾ. Al-Zajjāj gives lā taḥāḍḍūn and lā taḥāḍḍūna; al-Ṭabarī reports Kufan alif versus Basran no alif. Al-Durr calls ʿĀṣim's form lengthened and unhamzated."}, {"id": "89:17/q14/p3", "position": "Some readings omit the final yāʾ of 'honored me' and 'humiliated me'; Ibn ʿĀmir also doubles the dāl of qaddara.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports omission in continuation and pause, comparing a night-oath reading. Al-Bayḍāwī names Ibn ʿĀmir, Kufans, and Abū ʿAmr for omission in both settings and Nāfiʿ in pause; he separately reports Ibn ʿĀmir's doubled dāl."}, {"id": "89:17/q14/p4", "position": "The inheritance wording evokes gathering, consuming, and attachment to wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī derives turāth from wirāth by replacing initial wāw with tāʾ, like wijāh. Al-Layth glosses lamm as forceful gathering (troop or stones); al-Rāzī says 'intense eating' is only a paraphrase. Al-Zajjāj reads voracious gathering of orphan inheritance; al-Ḥasan says heirs merge their own and the orphan's shares; another view includes lawful, doubtful, and unlawful estate parts. Al-Kashshāf instead focuses on idle heirs wasting unearned inheritance on lavish food. Rāzī glosses jamm as abundance and excessive love of wealth; Abū ʿAmr explains it as 'increases.'"}]}

{"id": "89:18/q03", "question": "Whom does the unexpressed object of urging include?", "turns_on": "Whether the transitive verb has an understood object or is used without one.", "positions": [{"id": "89:18/q03/p1", "position": "It can include oneself, one's family, or other people.", "reasons": "NAHHAS says listeners understand the omitted object as others. {"id": "89:18/q04", "question": "What does ṭaʿām mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether ṭaʿām denotes feeding as an act, food supplied through an omitted expression, or provision in a broader sense.", "positions": [{"id": "89:18/q04/p1", "position": "It is the act of feeding.", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA, ALUSI and IBNASHUR allow ṭaʿām as a verbal noun; ALUSI compares ʿaṭāʾ for giving. {"id": "89:18/q05", "question": "Who is the miskīn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:18/q05/p1", "position": "A poor or needy person, broadly including the poor.", "reasons": "ALUSI explicitly includes both needy and poor. {"id": "89:18/q06", "question": "What does failure to urge imply about one's own giving?", "turns_on": "Whether exhortation is a sign of one's own giving, an act valued beyond individual giving, or the inward motive itself.", "positions": [{"id": "89:18/q06/p1", "position": "It implies that they fail to feed the poor themselves.", "reasons": "BURSEVI says failure to urge makes their own failure more blameworthy. IBNASHUR reasons that people unwilling even to advocate will not give, and that exhorting an act can stand for doing it when able; he compares mutual counsel to truth and patience in 103:3. BIQAI says urging is greater than giving because exhortation entails giving, while giving need not spur others."}, {"id": "89:18/q06/p2", "position": "The lack of urging also means there is no inward impulse to feed.", "reasons": "ASAD-NOTES compares 107:3 and construes the phrase as absence of the urge to feed the needy."}]}
{"id": "89:18/q07", "question": "How does this rebuke answer the claims about wealth and poverty?", "turns_on": "Whether the correction chiefly identifies obedience and neglect as true honor and disgrace, or calls for constant praise in either condition.", "positions": [{"id": "89:18/q07/p1", "position": "Wealth and poverty test people; real disgrace lies in neglect of the vulnerable and disobedience.", "reasons": "TAB reports Qatāda: honor comes through obedience, disgrace through disobedience; al-Ṭabarī prefers this because 89:17–19 name the conduct.
